items.headline: 厄文威爾許新作獲好評
items.context: 蘇格蘭作家厄文・威爾許（Irvine Welsh）推出新作《Can Nothing Save Us?》，描寫美國家庭在世代觀念分裂下的衝突，被譽為他晚期創作的代表作之一。Netflix改編1901年小說《我的璀璨事業》（My Brilliant Career），由菲莉帕・諾斯伊斯特（Phillipa Northeast）主演，獲得好評。

sources.summary: The Scottish author focuses on gun culture and generational conflict in this darkly satirical tale about a great power in decline “Why expect unconditional love from somebody you’ve brought into a fucked, dying planet, who then has to sit around and watch you screw it up even more?” So muses twentysomething college dropout Luke Ayrton on his parental lineage as he works the Las Vegas Strip, “comping girls for clubs” in Sin City. His job is to trawl the “plankton” of bacherlorette parties in order to lure the “whales” – rich men willing to spend to try to impress young women. “In this game your sociology skills sharpened,” it’s observed, but beyond the seedy side hustle lie weightier concerns: the matter of his family legacy. Electronic dance music aficionado and aspiring writer Luke is estranged from his Maga-positive Mom and Dad, and now lives with grandparents George and Molly, affluent boomers with a countercultural past. sources.summary: Phillipa Northeast is brilliant as a young woman rebelling against society’s expectations in 1890s Australia. It is witty, intelligent and absolutely glorious to watch “I’m hot headed, with a snub nose, and that’s why I prefer a direct gaze.” So speaks Sybylla, the charmingly irrepressible and irrepressibly charming heroine of My Brilliant Career, played utterly convincingly and with vim, vigour and joy by Philippa Northeast in the new adaptation of Miles Franklin’s 1901 Australian classic of the same name. Creator Liz Doran must have wept with happiness when they found an actor capable of bringing so much to an already glorious script – and who embodies the joie de vivre upon which so much of the plot, as everyone she meets becomes part of her orbit, depends. sources.summary: Now living with multiple sclerosis, Six rants about the masturbation film distributors won’t touch and the money mystery behind his horror hit Fifteen years ago, Dutch film-maker Tom Six succeeded where almost everybody fails – particularly in the world of horror. He actually shocked people. No self-respecting sophisticate admits to being shocked, of course, and no horror connoisseur will admit to being really and truly horrified. But Six really did freak audiences out with his extreme exploitation nightmare The Human Centipede, the first of a trilogy. It was a grenade in the faces of prim conformists, and also those badass horror fans who thought they’d seen it all. The “human centipede” of the title is created by a sadistic surgeon who imprisons three young people in a basement and sews them together mouth-to-anus as a vivisectional experiment. Six himself had been a director on the original Dutch TV show Big Brother that started the global franchise, and it was easy to see how his movie masterwork was intended as a satire on consumerist voyeurism and cruelty. Or maybe it just sprang from the same dark creative place that gave birth to the TV phenomenon of the age. Continue reading...

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Summerhall, Edinburgh Vengeance for a slaughtered pig is the starting point for a riotous parody that suggests the meat industry poses an existential threat to human survival That’s my next hotdog ruined. Shakespeare’s “too solid flesh” is squeezed into a sausage-shaped form in Mary Higgins and Ell Potter’s inventively guilt-trippy new show. Leaping wildly from Hamlet, this outrageous, confrontational performance-activism layers hooting comedy with world-ending dread as Mary (a vegan) attempts to persuade Potter (nicknamed “the sausage queen” by their dad) to change their meat-eating ways. Transposing Hamlet’s existential questions to the future survival of humanity via the meat industry’s impact on the planet, Higgins takes on the role of our stubborn, sauntering prince, seeking vengeance for the ghost of a poor, slaughtered, strangely seductive pig. Suave and silly, Potter is both ghost and Gertrude, the latter reading madness into the truth only her son is brave enough to face. items.context: 英國藝文界本週有三則新評論：愛丁堡藝穗節推出以1605年火藥陰謀案為題材的舞台劇《The Plot》；Prime Video紀錄片《An Amputation Obsession》，講述一名外科醫師因截肢戀癖切除自己雙腿的真實案件；美國歌手雀兒喜・沃爾夫（Chelsea Wolfe）推出新專輯《The Dark》。

英國藝文界本週有三則新評論。

愛丁堡藝穗節（Summerhall）推出舞台劇《The Plot》，以1605年火藥陰謀案的湯瑪士與羅伯特・溫特（Thomas and Robert Wintour）兄弟為主角，想像兩人死後在煉獄中回顧這場失敗政變。Prime Video紀錄片《An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon》，講述外科醫師尼爾・霍柏（Neil Hopper）因截肢戀癖切除自己雙腿的真實案件。美國歌手雀兒喜・沃爾夫（Chelsea Wolfe）推出新專輯《The Dark》，延續她過去以睡眠癱瘓經驗為靈感的陰暗曲風。

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Summerhall, Edinburgh Set in purgatory, Emma Howlett’s two-hander rethinks the national intrigue with 5 November Never play with matches is good advice – especially when gunpowder is involved. That the historical figures of Thomas and Robert Wintour begin this two-hander testing each other’s capacity to endure a naked flame suggests they have a high tolerance for risk. It is not clear if there are still explosives lying around, but they should know better. Not that it matters any more. These two Catholic brothers have sussed they must be in purgatory, their plot to blow up parliament having been foiled. Their accounts of what happened next are fuzzy, but they both remember being sentenced to death. They are not happy about their fate, but feel even more sympathy for the mercenary stooge known as Guy Fawkes, who has had to carry the can. Continue reading...

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: This documentary follows the shocking case of Neil Hopper, a top surgeon who had his own legs removed due to a fetish. No fetish or obsession is unique, and the internet can always connect you with others whose minds work the same way. It’s one of the great blessings and curses of the digital age, and central to An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon, a two-part documentary on which the “contains material some viewers may find disturbing” disclaimer is no exaggeration. We begin at the Royal Cornwall hospital, known locally as Treliske, in Truro, Cornwall. It used to have a man on its staff who was a minor medical superstar: Neil Hopper, a vascular surgeon, was well known for his clinical expertise and comforting bedside manner, particularly when advising on and performing amputations. He acquired full hero status in 2019, when he was diagnosed with sepsis and had both legs amputated below the knee but miraculously returned to work within six months, astonishing physiotherapists and other medical professionals with how well he adapted to disability. An Amputation Obsession: the Monster and the Surgeon is on Prime Video Continue reading...

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: (Loma Vista) The genre-blending Californian artist casts off past toxic influences with a powerful set of tender, brooding and emotionally charged songs that wouldn’t feel out of place as festival anthems When Chelsea Wolfe was interviewed by the Guardian in 2015 about her fourth album, Abyss, she revealed that her music had been informed by the bouts of sleep paralysis she’d suffered from since childhood. The condition – a transitional state between being awake and asleep – affects sufferers in different ways. Some wake up feeling paralysed, others see ghosts or demonic figures. For the California-born singer-songwriter, it meant “waking up, and you can move your body and your eyes are open, but there are figures and people from your dreams still present in your room”. No surprise, then, that her music – a blend of drone, alt, folk, industrial and doom metal – had ended up so spookily unsettling. She appeared on album covers with pupil-less eyes, spoke in interviews about “following the path of witchcraft” and even covered Norwegian black metal act and convicted arsonist/murderer Burzum. She did have a sense of humour about it all, however, telling one interviewer, with a chuckle: “It’s not party music.” Since then, though, much has changed. Wolfe left Los Angeles for the mountains above the city – where she’s finally been able to enjoy a good night’s sleep. Sobriety since 2021 has also brought what she calls “a new clarity”. Both developments inform The Dark. Continue reading...

sources.summary: My father, Jack Crabtree, who has died aged 87, was a figurative painter whose work gave dignity to people whose lives were often overlooked. He developed a distinctive form of social realism, rooted in his working-class upbringing and driven by a belief that every person had a story worth telling. He painted miners, steelworkers, industrial communities and ordinary people caught up in extraordinary circumstances. Born in Rochdale, the son of Lilian, a cotton mill worker, and Roland Crabtree, a labourer at the gasworks, Jack discovered art almost by accident. A schoolteacher at Rochdale grammar school for boys encouraged him to try the subject, and a scholarship eventually took him from Rochdale College of Art in 1955 to St Martin’s School of Art in 1957, then the Royal Academy Schools from 1959 to 1961. sources.name: The Guardian
sources.summary: Throughout his many years working at the British Film Institute (BFI) and on its annual LGBTQ+ film festival, my friend and work associate Brian Robinson – who has died of brain cancer aged 67 – was celebrated as a champion of queer cinema. He was also a flamboyant showman who strode on to stages at the BFI Southbank with supreme confidence, establishing mischievous rapport with film-makers and audiences. Brian joined the BFI in London as a press officer in 1987, in 2000 becoming communications manager for archive and heritage. In the same year, he joined the programming team of the BFI’s London Lesbian & Gay film festival (retitled BFI Flare in 2014), stepping down only in 2024 after being diagnosed with glioblastoma. Over these several decades, he grew as an elder of London’s LGBTQ+ film community and a larger-than-life character with a rich social network. Continue reading...
